metaDescription: Six food processors that list at or below $200, from a 1.5-cup chopper to an 11-cup full-size, compared on motor, bowl, attachments and everyday upkeep.
expertTake: The Hamilton Beach 10-cup is the top pick under $200 for its built-in scraper and 450-watt motor. The 8-cup Black+Decker is the value pick for plain chopping on a tight budget. If you only need minced garlic and herbs, skip full-size machines and buy a 1.5-cup chopper.
introParagraphs: A $200 cap is generous for this category. It lets you buy a proper full-size machine with slicing and shredding discs, and most buyers do not need to spend more. The real question is what the money buys: capacity, a stronger motor, or a smarter bowl.

Prices move, and the $200 cap reflects listing prices at the time this guide was updated. Within the cap there are three tiers: tiny choppers, mid-size 8 to 10 cup machines, and one full-size 11-cup unit. We sort them by job so you can see where the budget is best spent.

products.name: Hamilton Beach 10-Cup Food Processor 450 W
products.description:
The standout detail here is the bowl scraper built into the lid. Turn it and the paddle sweeps the sides, which is exactly what a hummus or nut-butter batch needs and what you normally do with a spatula while the machine is stopped. It sits on a 450-watt motor, the practical entry point for a processor that can chew dense food.

A ten-cup bowl is two cups larger than the Black+Decker 8-cup and the Hamilton Beach 8-cup, which matters when you double a salsa recipe. Where it loses ground to the 11-cup Cuisinart is in the base weight and the slicing options, because it relies on two attachments instead of a full disc set. For most weeknight cooking that is plenty.

Ownership is easy. The Easy Clean bowl design reduces the number of crevices where food hides, and the bowl, lid and discs rinse quickly. Keep the scraper paddle clear of the blade when loading, and avoid thin liquids above the center post.
products.bestFor: Home cooks who make dips, nut butters and slaw and want the best mix of size and convenience under the cap.
pros: Built-in scraper reduces stopping to spatula
10-cup bowl is two cups larger than the 8-cup models
450 W motor handles dips and nut butters
Easy Clean bowl has few crevices
cons: Two attachments, not a full disc set
Scraper adds one more part to clean

products.name: Cuisinart Pro Custom 11-Cup Food Processor
products.description:
Stretching toward the cap buys you the biggest bowl on this list and a name with a long parts history. The 11-cup bowl is the only one here that handles a full head of cabbage in a single load, and its slicing and shredding discs make it the closest thing to a restaurant-style prep machine under $200.

The flip side is cost per job. If your cooking is mainly pulsed salsa and hummus, the 10-cup Hamilton Beach with its scraper gets you there for less and with fewer parts. The Cuisinart earns its place when slicing consistency and sheer volume matter.

Parts are dishwasher-safe by the maker's description, so the bowl and lid can go on the top rack. Hand-wash the discs, dry them upright and store them in the bowl so the sharp edges are never loose in a drawer.
products.bestFor: Cooks who slice and shred in volume and want full-size capacity under the cap.
pros: Largest bowl in this lineup
Slicing and shredding discs included
Dishwasher-safe bowl and lid
Long-running design with parts support
cons: Costs more than the 450 W Hamilton Beach models

products.name: Hamilton Beach 8-Cup Food Processor 450 W
products.description:
Where its sibling has a scraper, this model has a large feed chute that takes a whole block of cheese. For shredding that is the better trade, because it saves the knife work and the second pass. It shares the 450-watt motor of the 10-cup model but in a more compact 8-cup bowl.

Choose it when cabinet space matters. The smaller bowl is easy to store, and it holds enough for a family's weeknight shredding and slicing. It will be outgrown by anyone who regularly doubles recipes, at which point the 10-cup version is the natural step.

Upkeep is straightforward: wash the bowl, lid and discs after each use and avoid overfilling, since stuffing the chute with hard cheese strains a 450-watt motor. Let it rest a minute between large shredding jobs.
products.bestFor: Shredding cheese and vegetables for a small family where cabinet space is limited.
pros: Large chute fits a whole cheese block
450 W motor matches the 10-cup model
Compact bowl stores easily
Quick shredding with little pre-cutting
cons: Eight cups is tight for double batches

products.name: Black+Decker 8-Cup Food Processor 450 W
products.description:
This one earns the value badge by getting the basics right at a low tier. A 450-watt motor and a stainless S-blade give it the same chopping ability as the pricier Hamilton Beach models. Assembly is clever: the bowl sits on the base and the lid itself acts as the locking mechanism, so there are fewer parts to line up.

Attachments are the trade. It comes with discs for shredding and slicing, but its feature list is leaner than the 10-cup Hamilton Beach or the Cuisinart 11-cup. If you want a nut butter or a salsa on a budget, it delivers. If you want adjustable slicing, look higher.

Plastic bowls scratch and cloud with time, so keep metal utensils out of the bowl. Wash the S-blade by hand to keep it sharp, and do not let hot liquids go in unless the manual allows it.
products.bestFor: Shoppers who want a working 8-cup processor at a low tier for chopping, salsa and dips.
pros: 450 W motor at a low tier
Lid doubles as the locking mechanism
Stainless S-blade for chopping and mixing
Handles salsa, hummus and nut butter
cons: Leaner attachment set than pricier models

products.name: Savorfuze Dual 8-Cup Bowl Food Chopper

specList.label: Bowls
specList.value: 8 cups glass plus 8 cups second bowl

specList.label: Speeds
specList.value: Low and high, press to run

products.description:
This is a chopper rather than a disc processor, and the two eight-cup bowls are its selling point: one glass, one second bowl, so you can chop raw and cooked foods back to back without washing. It runs on a two-speed press-and-hold control, where releasing the button stops the blades.

It is designed for mincing vegetables, small batches of boneless meat and purees. It does not slice or shred, so compare it to the 1.5-cup chopper rather than the full-size units. The glass bowl resists odors, which suits onion and garlic work, while the second bowl is lighter for lifting.

Keep batches modest and let the motor cool between runs. Chill meat before mincing, wash the blade assembly carefully and let the glass bowl cool before rinsing.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want a roomy chopper with two bowls for prep without cross-flavors.
pros: Two eight-cup bowls reduce washing between jobs
Glass bowl resists lingering odors
Press-and-hold speeds for texture control
Minces small batches of boneless meat
cons: Press-and-hold control tires the thumb on long runs

products.name: Black+Decker 1.5-Cup Electric Chopper 150 W
products.description:
It is the cheapest machine in the lineup and also the smallest, built for herbs, bread crumbs and quick fruit chops. A bi-level stainless blade sweeps two heights of the bowl, which helps a small bowl produce an even result without a spatula pass.

Its 150-watt motor limits it to soft and small items. Pit a handful of olives or crumb a slice of bread and it is fine, but a carrot needs pre-cutting. Next to the Savorfuze with its dual 8-cup bowls, this one wins on size and loses on capacity.

Cleanup is its charm: removable parts are listed as dishwasher-safe, and the whole unit stores in a drawer. Pulse in short taps rather than holding the button, because the little motor heats quickly.
products.bestFor: Quick small jobs such as herbs, garlic and crumbs, or as a second machine beside a bigger one.
pros: Smallest and cheapest option here
Bi-level blade evens out a tiny bowl
One-touch pulse is simple
Fits in a drawer
cons: 150 W motor limits it to soft food

buyingCriteria.explanation: At this cap you can reach a full-size 11-cup machine like the Cuisinart Pro Custom 11, so paying more is rarely needed for home use. The lower tiers split into 450-watt 8 to 10 cup units such as the Hamilton Beach pair and the Black+Decker 8-cup, plus tiny choppers. Spend toward the cap only when you need volume and a full disc set.

A 450-watt base runs the 10-cup and 8-cup Hamilton Beach and the 8-cup Black+Decker comfortably for salsa, slaw and dips. The 150-watt Black+Decker chopper stalls on carrots and hard cheese. Match wattage to the hardest food you will feed, not the easiest.

Eight cups suits two to four people, ten cups helps when doubling recipes, and eleven cups is for big batches. The 1.5-cup chopper is for single-clove or single-handful jobs. Oversizing a bowl just means a heavier machine to wash. A cook who pulses garlic for two will find the 8-cup Black+Decker perfectly roomy, while a batch cook who shreds cheese for a party should lean toward the 11-cup Cuisinart.

The Hamilton Beach 8-cup's large chute fits a block of cheese, while the 10-cup adds a bowl scraper built into the lid. Pick the chute for shredding days and the scraper for dips and nut butters. Few machines under this cap offer both.

Full-size units give you shredding and slicing discs, but the Savorfuze and the 1.5-cup chopper do not. If you slice cucumbers, potatoes or cabbage regularly, skip the choppers. A chopper is not a cheaper path to the same result.

Glass bowls such as the Savorfuze's resist odors but weigh more, while the plastic bowls on the Black+Decker 8-cup and Hamilton Beach machines are light and shatter-resistant. Plastic clouds after years of use. Rinse garlic and onion promptly in plastic, and give the bowl an occasional soak in warm water with a spoonful of baking soda to lift stubborn smells.

howWeEvaluated.title: Under-cap eligibility
howWeEvaluated.description: Every pick had to list at or below $200 at the time of update. We also kept the lineup to real food processors and choppers, not blenders or hand tools. Prices move, so treat the cap as a snapshot.

howWeEvaluated.title: Motor and bowl fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared 450-watt, 150-watt and unlisted-motor machines against their bowl volume. A strong motor in a small bowl ranked well for dense loads. A large bowl with a weak motor ranked as a light-duty tool.

howWeEvaluated.title: Attachment depth
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked which machines include slicing and shredding discs, which add a scraper, and which are chop-only. We also noted how many separate parts each one asks you to wash and store. The Cuisinart Pro Custom 11 and Hamilton Beach pair led here, while the Savorfuze and mini chopper were rated as specialists.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cleanup and storage
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed dishwasher-safe parts, crevice-free bowls and how a machine stores. The 1.5-cup chopper fits a drawer, while the 11-cup needs a shelf.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value inside the cap
howWeEvaluated.description: We ordered the six by price tier, from the 1.5-cup chopper up to the 11-cup Cuisinart, and asked what each step adds. The 10-cup Hamilton Beach is the sweet spot for features per dollar.

cards.text: The Hamilton Beach pair, the Black+Decker 8-cup and the Cuisinart 11-cup slice, shred and chop. They are bulkier but replace several kitchen tools.

cards.label: Chopper

cards.text: A bowl scraper or a wide bowl that lets you stop and stir. A 450-watt motor and a sharp S-blade help, and short runs prevent overheating.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Hamilton Beach 10-cup's built-in scraper is the best fit, and the Black+Decker 8-cup is the lower-cost alternative with the same motor.

maintenance.why: A soft brush keeps hands away from the edge. Drying promptly stops water spots on stainless.
Lower racks sit near the heating element and warp plastic. Rinse oily foods promptly.
Dust and splatter collect around the control. Never submerge the motor housing.
The motor will not start unless the lid is seated. Clean the lid tabs before blaming the motor.
A dull blade bruises herbs and loads the motor. Replace worn blades when chopping becomes uneven.

faq.q: Is a food processor under $200 good enough?
faq.a: Yes for almost all home cooking. A 450-watt 8 to 10 cup machine handles chopping, shredding and dips. Heavy dough and daily commercial-style use are where you would want more. The pricier tiers add motor headroom and parts support rather than better chopping, so most buyers are better off keeping the extra budget for good knives.

faq.q: Which is better, the 8-cup or the 10-cup?
faq.a: The 10-cup Hamilton Beach adds two cups and a built-in scraper, which helps with thick dips. The 8-cup models have a larger feed chute or a lower cost and take less cabinet space.

faq.q: Can I use a food processor for nut butter?
faq.a: Yes, but run it in short bursts and scrape the bowl. A 450-watt motor is the practical minimum. Let the motor cool between batches. Add a splash of neutral oil if the paste clumps, because a dry load asks the most of a 450-watt base.

faq.q: Is a chopper the same as a food processor?
faq.a: No. A chopper like the 1.5-cup Black+Decker or the Savorfuze only chops, minces and purees. A disc processor also slices and shreds.

faq.q: How long should a budget processor last?
faq.a: The motor base typically outlasts the bowl and lid. Hand-wash blades and avoid overloading. Expect to replace a cracked bowl before the motor fails. Keep the manual, since model numbers help when you order a lid or pusher, and store blades inside the bowl so they never rattle loose in a drawer.

faq.q: Do prices change within the cap?
faq.a: Yes. The $200 cap reflects listing prices when this guide was updated. Check the current listing before you buy. A model just above the cap today may dip below it in a sale, so use the cap as a guide to the tier rather than a promise.
